title: Shapiro–Wilk and graphical checks
biology: Cell biologists examine the distribution of time to lysis among independent cultured cells.
design: One lysis time for each independently treated culture; use a diagnostic to investigate shape.
data_characteristics: A distributional diagnostic, not the biological comparison
For models, examine residuals rather than pooled responses
other_examples: Distribution of a continuous trait within a group
question: Is a normal model a reasonable working description of these lysis times?
null: The independent observations come from a normal distribution.
options: Use a Q–Q plot alongside the test
Choose an analysis for the scientific target, not a p-value gate
assumptions: A normal population is the reference
Diagnostic sensitivity changes with sample size
parametric: Model positive skew with log-normal or gamma errors
Consider a meaningful transformation and check its new interpretation
nonparametric: Ranks can address a different distributional question
Bootstrap uncertainty can retain the mean target

plot_args.note: Keep the response and units explicit

practice: Would a nonsignificant Shapiro–Wilk result prove that these known log-normal data are normal?
code_simulate:
set.seed(1111)
d <- data.frame(culture = 1:36,
                lysis_minutes = rlnorm(36, log(45), .5))
write.csv(d, file.path(output_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
qqnorm(d$lysis_minutes, pch = 21, bg = "#246A73", col = "white",
       main = "", xlab = "Theoretical normal quantiles", ylab = "Lysis time (minutes)")
qqline(d$lysis_minutes, col = "#B7663E", lwd = 2)
generating_model: 36 independent lysis times follow a log-normal distribution with meanlog log(45) and log-scale SD 0.5.
generating_truth: The population is log-normal and positively skewed, not normal. The population geometric mean is 45 minutes.
teaching_point: A diagnostic explains how a working model misses the data; its p-value should not automatically select the scientific analysis.
